title: A Second Life for the Moon
dek: Inside a theatre-materials depot, reuse depends on labels, labour and permission as much as imagination.
disclosure: Original fictional feature. All people, places, quotations and ledger figures were authored for this exercise.

sections.heading: The door is wider than the office
paragraphs: At seven in the morning, a painted moon comes through the loading door sideways. It is taller than the person carrying it and too fragile to put down on its edge. Someone brings two padded blocks. Someone else moves a tea mug. For a minute, everything in the depot is organised around getting a moon safely onto the floor.

This is the ordinary work of Second Life, a fictional materials depot serving small theatres in the equally fictional town of Bellweather. Sets arrive after their final performance, when their makers are tired and the hire van is due back. What looked convincing under stage light becomes a pile of timber, hinges and awkward questions. Who owns it? What is it coated with? Can it be taken apart without destroying the useful part?

The depot is sometimes described as a place that saves things. Its coordinator, Mara Venn, prefers a less heroic account. “We keep things available,” she says. “Saving them is what the next person manages to do.” That distinction runs through the building, from the intake form to the shelf where unclaimed handles wait in jars.

sections.heading: A useful object needs a description
paragraphs: Every arrival gets an intake card. Dimensions are measured again even if they are written on the van sheet. Staff record the known material, visible damage, any declared coating and whether the owner permits alteration. “Plywood” is useful information. “Probably plywood” belongs in a different box. Unknown coatings are never magically turned into known ones by being donated.

Objects with unclear handling requirements go into a hold area pending an appropriate assessment. This is not a tutorial for deciding whether a material is safe. The depot's working rule is simply that uncertainty travels with the object until someone qualified can resolve it. A beautiful door with an incomplete history may spend longer on hold than a battered crate with a legible label.

The card is also a small act of translation. A designer looking for a palace window may search by shape. A carpenter may search by clear opening, fixing points or whether the frame will survive another move. Second Life keeps the theatrical description but adds the ordinary one: “arched window, no glazing, frame 180 by 90 centimetres.” A thing can keep its story without being trapped inside it.

sections.heading: The shelves are an argument
paragraphs: There is no room to store everything. The depot occupies a former delivery garage with one wide bay, a dry room and a narrow office. Floor space is allocated to things that are bulky, likely to be borrowed and difficult to source elsewhere. Small fittings live in drawers whose contents can be counted. A duplicate might be useful insurance or an object nobody has admitted is surplus.

Once a month, the staff walk the shelves without taking reservations. They look for items that have not moved, items whose labels no longer make sense, and items that have migrated into the wrong category. The walk is not a popularity contest. A rarely borrowed accessible entrance platform may justify its footprint because making one at short notice is expensive. Six nearly identical decorative plinths may not.

The staff ask prospective borrowers what they had to buy because they could not find it here. That list complicates the shelves. The most picturesque donations attract attention; the most useful requests often concern plain lengths of material, stable bases and transport cases. A depot built only from the photographs of its contents would be a very different institution.

sections.heading: What the ledger can say
paragraphs: The six-month ledger beside this article records completed loans and the measured mass leaving and returning during each month. It is an invented teaching dataset, not a report from a real organisation. March through May form the spring group; June through August form the summer group. The switch on the ledger changes that window and nothing else.

These numbers answer a narrow question: how much recorded activity passed through the door? They do not count unique objects. A door borrowed twice contributes twice to outgoing mass. A return in August may belong to a loan made in May. Subtracting the two columns does not tell us how much material was discarded, nor does it establish a carbon saving. There is no emissions calculation hidden behind the totals.

The busiest month by loan count is not the heaviest by outgoing mass. In June, many small school-production kits went out. In July, fewer borrowers collected several large scenic units. Both workloads matter, but they place different demands on staff. The point of publishing the table is to let that difference remain visible instead of reducing the season to one triumphant number.

sections.heading: Permission to cut
paragraphs: A borrowed chair is expected to come back as a chair. A sheet of material offered for adaptation may return as several smaller pieces, or may be used up entirely under a separate transfer agreement. Second Life labels these arrangements differently. A loan is not a vague promise that something of roughly equal value will eventually reappear.

For a designer, permission to alter can matter more than pristine condition. A scarred panel that can be drilled is more useful than a perfect panel that cannot. The depot asks owners to settle this before an object goes on the shelf. Staff should not have to negotiate the meaning of “look after it” while a borrower is loading a van.

This also changes how repairs are documented. Replacing a missing hinge keeps an object working. Changing the size of an opening changes what it is. Both may be reasonable, but the next borrower needs to know which happened. The label is a continuing description rather than a certificate of original purity.

sections.heading: The cost of keeping things available
paragraphs: Borrowers see a shelf. Behind it are appointments, lifting plans, photographs, label printing, interrupted lunches and a surprising amount of sweeping. A donated object can be free at the loading door and expensive by the time someone can borrow it. The depot has started recording handling time alongside its accounts, though those incomplete records are not included in this article's ledger.

Volunteer Ivo Pell calls the job “making the second use less mysterious.” He spends a morning matching loose fittings to their frames. None of it produces an impressive before-and-after picture. By lunchtime, however, three awkward objects have become things another person could confidently book. That confidence is a service, even when it looks like a bag of labelled bolts.

Second Life charges small borrowing fees and pays its coordinator. Volunteers extend the opening hours; they do not make staffing costs disappear. The depot's next funding request concerns a part-time intake role rather than a larger building. More space would allow more objects to wait. More skilled time might allow more of them to leave.

sections.heading: When the moon comes back
paragraphs: Three weeks after the morning delivery, the painted moon is collected for a youth production. Its new borrower asks to change the painted face but keep the frame. The owner has already agreed to repainting. The intake card records the permission; the outgoing card records a small split near one fixing point. Neither fact makes the object less magical under a light.

When it returns, the depot will check what changed, update its description and look for another place to put it. There is no guarantee of a third production. Reuse is a sequence of contingent acts: someone has to know the object exists, be able to collect it, and find that it fits. The shelf provides the possibility. The rest still takes work.
Outside, the van pulls away with the moon lying flat on a blanket. Inside, two empty padded blocks remain by the door. For once, the best evidence that the depot is useful is an absence.

notes.title: About the ledger
notes.text: Synthetic monthly transactions, March–August 2026. Mass rounded to whole kilograms at dispatch and return. Loans are completed outgoing bookings; returns can relate to earlier months. No unique-object, waste-diversion or emissions claim is supported.

notes.title: Loan and transfer
notes.text: A loan carries an expectation of return. A transfer permits material to be consumed or permanently altered under its own agreement; transfer data is not present in this ledger.
